title: Шеф становится су-шефом  (The Chef Becomes a Sous-Chef)

segments.t: In front of a crowd of guests and journalists in the dining room, Kristina introduces chef and author Valdemar Barani to begin his culinary masterclass. Barani announces his favorite signature meat roll and publicly needles Viktor Petrovich by calling him up to serve as his assistant.
Дамы и господа.
Шеф-повара и писателя Вальдемара Барани.
Господа, только я не буду много говорить.
А то вам будет неинтересно читать мою книгу.
Сегодня я хочу представить вам свое любимое блюдо.
Но мне понадобится помощник.
Виктор Петрович?
А как плезиром еще.
Наш шеф-повар только что стал су-шефом.
Лучше им не мешать.
Как говорится.
Ты смотри, а.
Хочет шефа публично унизить.
Now let's break down each line of their conversation.
Дамы и господа.
'Ladies and gentlemen.' Barinov offers the comeback to Vika: spoken Russian trims this down to just 3 words, dropping the extra helper words that English has to spell out.
Шеф-повара и писателя Вальдемара Барани.
'Chef and author Valdemar Barani.' Vika jumps in dryly beside Barinov, steering the talk right where she wants it.
Господа, только я не буду много говорить.
'Gentlemen, I am not going to talk too much.' Barinov underscores one classic term with Vika: "gospoda" means "gentlemen" (from "gospodin"), giving the line its exact edge.
А то вам будет неинтересно читать мою книгу.
'Otherwise it will not be interesting for you to read my book.' Vika chooses this vivid piece on cue: "neinteresno" means "uninteresting", and it carries the main weight of what Vika is saying.
Сегодня я хочу представить вам свое любимое блюдо.
'Today I want to present my favorite dish to you.' Barinov pushes back wryly with a sigh, without trying to dress up how he really feels.
Но мне понадобится помощник.
'But I am going to need an assistant.' Vika sharpens one practical term toward Barinov: "pomoshchnik" means "assistant", and it carries the main weight of what Vika is saying.
Виктор Петрович?
'Viktor Petrovich?' Vika lays out this line frankly here: Russian keeps the exact word order of a normal statement here, turning it into a question for Barinov purely through rising pitch at the end.
А как плезиром еще.
'With pleasure, of course.' Vika follows up warmly with a shrug, to clear the air between them once and for all.
Наш шеф-повар только что стал су-шефом.
'Our head chef just became a sous-chef.' Barinov stresses this vivid term toward Vika: "shef-povar" means "head chef", and it carries the main weight of what Barinov is saying.
Лучше им не мешать.
'It is better not to get in their way.' Vika lays out that line with candor: spoken Russian trims this down to just 4 words, dropping the extra helper words that English has to spell out.
Как говорится.
'As the saying goes.' Barinov speaks firmly as they talk, before Vika can change the subject.
Ты смотри, а.
'Just look at that.' Vika uses one sharp expression in earnest: "smotri" means "look" (from "smotret"), giving the line its exact edge.
Хочет шефа публично унизить.
'He wants to humiliate the Chef in public.' Barinov shares this line before Vika: spoken Russian trims this down to just 4 words, dropping the extra helper words that English has to spell out.

That wraps up this scene as valdemar Barani begins his public masterclass in the dining room and publicly humiliates Viktor Petrovich by inviting him up as his assistant. Until next time!
До завтра!
